prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the Melexis MLX91219 current sensor (SOIC‑8, –40 °C to 125 °C) through an external MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0 (spidev0.0) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling once per second, logs each reading with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named current_log.txt, and drives a cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) HIGH when the measured current exceeds a defined threshold and LOW otherwise; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect SPI transfer failures, and treat ADC values of all‑zero or all‑ones as a sensor‑absent condition, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, and ensure the fan is turned OFF, using the appropriate driver interface for all GPIO control, opening the GPIO chip by name and attempting the Pi 5 specific API call before falling back to chip 0, and include stdint.h along with any other required standard headers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a Honeywell/SGX MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor (dual‑element MOS, NO2/CO) via I2C bus 1, using an external 16‑bit ADC such as an ADS1115 or a simulated 16‑bit raw reading, converts the raw CO resistance value to a concentration in ppm with a calibrated logarithmic curve, and logs each timestamped ppm value to a file named co_log.txt every 5 seconds; the program must verify successful driver library initialization, creation of the I2C handle, and detect any I2C read failures that indicate a missing sensor or bus error, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY‑026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO 4 (BCM) for flame presence, routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0, and connecting the MCP3008 chip‑select to CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM) with SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM); the program must log once per second to a timestamped CSV file named flame_data.csv containing the flame presence flag (1/0) and a temperature reading, must validate driver library initialization, SPI handle creation, each SPI transfer, and all file I/O, skipping any entry and printing an error to stderr when the sensor is absent or a SPI bus error occurs, and must cleanly release all resources on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), using the driver library for all GPIO and SPI operations and not employing any other software library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the SGX Sensortech MICS-4514 dual MOS sensor (CO/NO2) over the I2C bus, extracts the two 16‑bit ADC readings (OX for CO and RED for NO2) from the four‑byte response, converts the OX value to a CO concentration in ppm, and every 5 seconds appends the CO ppm value to a file named co_log.txt while also checking whether the value meets or exceeds a 25 ppm alert threshold and, if so, writing an alert entry to a separate file named alert_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for I2C initialization failures, read errors, and any file‑I/O problems, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, thereby simulating an industrial air‑quality monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads sound pressure levels from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU analog MEMS microphones, using a bit‑banged I2C emulation on bus 1 with the analog OUT signals connected to GPIO2/BCM2 and GPIO3/BCM3, samples each microphone every 100 ms, computes the average level, and appends a timestamped entry of that average to a file named audio_log.txt; if a read from either sensor fails the program must log an error value of –999.0 dB for that sample and continue operation, and it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples audio from two Analog Devices ADMP401 MEMS microphones using an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, with chip‑select lines CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) and CE1 on GPIO9 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), while driving an LED on GPIO27 (BCM); the program must acquire one sample from each microphone every 1 ms for a total window of 100 ms (100 samples per channel), compute the RMS level for each channel, log the window timestamp together with mic1 RMS and mic2 RMS to a file named audio_events.csv, trigger the LED to stay on for 500 ms whenever either RMS exceeds a high‑level threshold, include error handling for SPI initialization failures and file I/O errors, and cleanly handle a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples the analog output of a Melexis MLX91204 Hall effect current sensor using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2 BCM, SCL on GPIO3 BCM), reading single‑ended on channel A0 at a rate of 10 Hz, converting the raw values to current, storing each converted reading in a circular buffer of 100 elements, and triggering a warning LED on GPIO17 BCM whenever the average of the buffered currents exceeds a 50.0 A threshold; the implementation must employ the driver library I2C API functions for raw register operations, include robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C reads, and sensor‑absent conditions, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the LED and releases all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit TCS34725 I2C color sensor on I2C bus 1, initializing the sensor through the supplied driver, waiting at least 3 ms after power‑on before any read, then reading the clear, red, green and blue values once every second and appending a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,clear,red,green,blue” to a file named color_log.csv, creating the file with a header row if it does not already exist; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write, printing a warning to stderr on a transient failure and continuing, but if three consecutive I2C operations fail it should exit gracefully, and it must exit with a non‑zero code if the driver initialization or I2C open fails or if the sensor’s ID register does not match the expected value; on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program must close the I2C handle, flush and close the CSV file, and invoke the driver’s cleanup call, and it must implement the one‑second interval without using a blocking sleep that would prevent signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog values from two Seeed Studio Grove Moisture Sensors using an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 via the driver library /dev/spidev0.0, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); sensor 1 is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 and sensor 2 to channel 1, the program must sample both sensors every 5 seconds, log each reading with a timestamp to a file named moisture_log.csv containing the header “Timestamp,Moisture1,Moisture2”, verify that all SPI and driver initialization calls succeed, gracefully handle cases where a sensor is absent or the SPI bus reports an error, and ensure that on any exit path triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM the SPI file descriptors and driver library resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Melexis MLX91211 Triaxis Current Sensor (analog ratiometric Hall‑effect) through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), with the MLX91211 analog output connected to MCP3008 channel 0 and a motor shutdown control on GPIO17 (BCM); the program must sample the current once every second, convert the ADC reading to amperes, write a line containing a timestamp and the current in amperes to a file named current_log.csv (adding a header if the file is new or empty), check all open, ioctl, read and file I/O calls for errors and retry any SPI communication failures up to three times, and implement error handling and graceful termination by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM to close file descriptors and release GPIO lines cleanly; if the measured current exceeds 10.0 A the software must drive GPIO17 low to disable the motor, log the over‑current event, wait one second, then drive GPIO17 high to re‑enable the motor, and continue normal sampling thereafter.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Melexis MLX90817 absolute pressure sensor on I2C bus 1, reading the sensor once per second and appending each measurement to a file named pressure_log.csv that is opened once at startup with a header row and flushed after every write; each CSV line must contain an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the pressure in kPa, and the program must check every I2C call and every file operation for errors, printing to stderr the register and the driver error code on any I2C read failure while continuing without logging, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or repeated read failures, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Melexis MLX90834 pressure sensor (SENT‑only MEMS) through an ADS1115 ADC bridge on the I2C bus, reading the pressure channel on AIN0 and the NTC temperature channel on AIN1 in single‑ended mode, validating every driver call and retrying any failed I2C read up to three times while handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, then printing the pressure in kPa and temperature in °C to the console once per second, driving a warning LED on GPIO17 (active‑high) HIGH whenever the pressure exceeds 105.0 kPa, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads motor current from a Melexis MLX91209 Hall‑effect current sensor (analog output) using an MCP3008 10‑bit SPI ADC on bus SPI0 CE0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, with CE on GPIO8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), sampling the sensor’s analog output on MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) every 100 ms, logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named current_log.txt in append mode and flushing after every write, handling driver library initialization failures, SPI open or transfer errors, invalid ADC values and file I/O errors, asserting GPIO27 (BCM) HIGH to shut down the motor when the measured current exceeds 10 A, logging an OVERCURRENT event and terminating the program in that case, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly closing the SPI handle, closing the log file, resetting GPIO27 to LOW and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Honeywell MICROceL MCO‑S4 CO sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (1 MHz, mode 0) using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM), sampling channel 0 once per second, and after each successful read logs the timestamp and voltage to a file named co_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,Voltage: X.XX V”; the program must check the return values of the required library API calls and the SPI transfer function, and if an SPI transfer fails it must log the error, wait one second before retrying, and ensure the alarm connected to GPIO 4 (BCM) is turned off for safety, while under normal operation it drives GPIO 4 HIGH when the measured voltage exceeds 2.5 V and LOW otherwise, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI handle, close the log file, turn off the alarm, and invoke the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors methane concentration using a Honeywell MICROpeL Model 41000-020 Combustible Gas Sensor (analog output) interfaced through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI bus 0, channel 0, configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, with VDD/VREF tied to the Pi 3.3 V pin 1, DGND/AGND to any Pi ground, CLK on GPIO11 (SCLK, BCM), DOUT on GPIO9 (MISO, BCM), DIN on GPIO10 (MOSI, BCM) and CS/SHDN on GPIO8 (CE0, BCM); the program must read the sensor once per second, log each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to “methane_log.txt” in append mode, and write a visible leak alarm to stderr whenever the concentration exceeds 1000 ppm, while checking the library’s API call() three separate times, as well as checking fopen() and localtime_r() for errors, logging any SPI transfer failure to stderr and continuing operation rather than crashing; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, and closing any open file handle, and must obey the constraint of not using the driver library directly, instead using the driver’s negative‑handle error codes without invoking the library’s API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure data from a Melexis MLX90830 analog pressure sensor using an ADS1115 16‑bit ADC on I2C bus 1, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM) and the sensor’s analog output wired to ADS1115 channel AIN0, sampling at a rate of 1 Hz, validating that each reading falls within the 0‑100 kPa range, logging each valid pressure value together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt, performing thorough error handling for all I2C and ADC initialization and read operations, detecting and handling conditions such as a missing sensor or bus errors, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the program receives a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the analog Honeywell HIH-4602-A humidity sensor (which includes an integral thermistor) through an MCP3208 12‑bit ADC connected on the SPI0 bus using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) as the chip‑select line, reads the humidity and temperature values, appends each reading as a comma‑separated line containing a timestamp, humidity, and temperature to a file named humidity_log.txt, and when the humidity value exceeds an 80 % threshold triggers an email alert via ssmtp; the implementation must include robust error handling for the ADC driver initialization, any SPI transfer failures, and all file I/O operations, and must also ensure that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

/*
 * Si1172-A30-GMR Heart Rate / SpO₂ sensor reader for Raspberry Pi Zero W.
 *
 * The Si1172 requires a proprietary algorithm to convert raw PPG samples
 * to true HR and SpO₂.  This program reads the raw 16-bit IR and RED ADC
 * values and logs them as proxy values for HR and SpO₂, documenting
 * this limitation in comments.  A read error is always logged with an
 * error flag (0 = OK, 1 = read error, 2 = sensor absent / uninitialized).
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   Si1172 SDA  -> GPIO 2 (I2C bus 1)
 *   Si1172 SCL  -> GPIO 3 (I2C bus 1)
 *   Si1172 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   Si1172 GND  -> GND
 *
 * Build:
 *   gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o si1172_hr si1172_hr.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:
 *   sudo ./si1172_hr
 */

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that opens the CSI camera exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2 on the /dev/video0 bus, configures exactly four buffers sized according to the documented YUYV format, captures video frames, fragments each frame into UDP datagrams not exceeding 65 000 bytes, and prefixes each datagram with a header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragments, and payload size before sending the packets to a specified target IP and port; the program must invoke the required API calls on the command line as `./program <the library's API call> <the library's API call>`, rigorously check the result of every system call (open, ioctl, mmap, socket, sendto, etc.) and exit gracefully on error, run continuously until it receives SIGINT or SIGTERM, and then cleanly stop streaming, unmap all buffers and close every opened descriptor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0 in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK), queries the device capabilities to ensure both V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are present, sets the pixel format to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG with a width of 192 (the documented value) and V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests four MMAP buffers, starts streaming, dequeues a single frame, verifies that the dequeued buffer’s bytesused field is greater than zero, and writes the raw MJPEG bytes directly to a file named image.jpg without any re‑encoding; every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen call must have its return value checked and any failure reported with a descriptive perror/errno message, and a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to stop streaming, unmap all buffers, free the buffer array, close the file and the device file descriptor on all exit paths, ensuring clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using the board’s GPIO software PWM bus and four active‑low push‑buttons with internal pull‑ups, where the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), the tilt‑up button to GPIO6 (BCM), the tilt‑down button to GPIO7 (BCM), the pan‑left button to GPIO8 (BCM) and the pan‑right button to GPIO9 (BCM); the program must generate a 50 Hz PWM period (20 ms) with pulse widths ranging from 1 ms to 2 ms (corresponding to duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000), initialize both servos to the mid‑position value 75, and on each button press adjust the corresponding axis by ±5 while clamping the position to the range 25–125, poll the button states every 50 ms, check the return status of every driver call and handle any request failures, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly release all allocated resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm 64‑bit that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0, uses select() with a 2‑second timeout to wait for a frame, requests buffers, memory‑maps them, queues a buffer, starts streaming, dequeues the captured frame, stops streaming, unmaps the buffers, frees them and closes the file descriptor, handling SIGINT so that all these steps are performed cleanly on interruption; the captured image, originally in the documented YUYV format, must be converted to RGB24, processed with a blur filter, then encoded as a JPEG file named capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg with quality set to 75, and every system call and memory allocation must be checked for failure with error messages printed to stderr and all resources released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75031 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends each reading to a file named depth_log.csv, creating a CSV header row if the file is newly created and writing timestamped distance values; the program must verify successful initialization of the sensor interface, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C read/write transaction, and all file operations, and if an I2C read fails it must log a row with distance ‑1, attempt to re‑open the I2C handle, and continue sampling, while also handling SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates the sensor interface without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient‑light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 proximity/ambient‑light sensor attached to I2C bus 1, sampling every 500 ms, and appends each reading to a file named biometric_log.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the program must handle I2C read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and if the sensor is absent or initialization fails it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, while also installing a SIGINT handler that, upon receipt, cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s library API call() before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor on I2C bus 1 to measure distance, waiting approximately 50 ms after each trigger before reading the result and sampling every 200 ms; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus, verify each write and read operation as well as the file open for logging, and on any I2C error print a diagnostic message and skip to the next sample without crashing, while logging each successful reading in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>” to a file named distance_log.txt and also printing the same line to stdout, using a fixed‑size local buffer for the timestamp to avoid dynamic allocation, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by exiting the sampling loop, closing the I2C handle, the log file, and shutting down the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO 17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 18 (BCM), to detect object proximity and log the binary readings (0 or 1) together with timestamps every 100 milliseconds to a file named obstacle_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for any GPIO setup failures, and if a sensor read fails it should write an error message to stderr while continuing operation, and it must also handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense ICU‑20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling every 100 ms, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) such that the LED is turned on when the measured distance is below 20 cm and off otherwise, while logging each distance reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the implementation must check the result of every I2C, driver library, and file operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and ensure that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

static int i2c_write_byte(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value)
{
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_byte(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *out)
{
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    uint8_t val;
    if (read(fd, &val, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *out = val;
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_word(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *out)
{
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read 16-bit from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *out = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_write_byte(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value)
{
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_byte(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *out)
{
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    uint8_t val;
    if (read(fd, &val, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *out = val;
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_word(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *out)
{
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read 16-bit from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *out = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Read a single byte from a register */
static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;

    if (read(fd, value, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

 * VL53L4CX time-of-flight distance reader for Raspberry Pi Zero W
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   VL53L4CX SDA  -> GPIO2 (I2C1 SDA, pin 3)
 *   VL53L4CX SCL  -> GPIO3 (I2C1 SCL, pin 5)
 *   VL53L4CX VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   VL53L4CX GND  -> GND
 *
 * Build:
 *   gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o vl53l4cx_reader vl53l4cx_reader.c -li2c
 *
 * Run:
 *   sudo ./vl53l4cx_reader

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a parking‑assist system using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and an SG90 servo connected on the GPIO bus, with the trigger line on GPIO 23 (BCM), the echo line on GPIO 24 (BCM) and the servo control line on GPIO 17 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, then repeatedly issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the echo while treating any condition where the echo line remains low or high for more than 50 ms as a sensor timeout that returns a sentinel error value and causes the reading to be skipped, map valid distances from 2 cm to 400 cm linearly to the servo angle range of –90° to +90° (2 cm → –90°, 400 cm → +90°) and invoke the library’s API call to set that angle, log each successful distance reading with a timestamp to a file named sensor_data.log appending each entry, run this loop every 200 ms until interrupted, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on receipt stop the library’s API call (pulse 0), release all resources and invoke the library’s API call on every exit path, ensuring that no GPIO operations occur after the library’s API call and that only valid BCM GPIO numbers are used (avoiding GPIO 28).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that repeatedly triggers distance readings from a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 every 50 ms using a 50 ms timing budget, logs each measured distance to a POSIX message queue, and activates a buzzer connected to GPIO23 (BCM) whenever the measured distance falls below 100 mm, while providing robust error handling for any I2C communication failures or sensor absence by gracefully handling all I2C read/write errors and ensuring that on receipt of a SIGINT the program cleanly releases the I2C handle, the message queue, the GPIO resources and any driver state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements an interrupt‑driven parking sensor using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus with the trigger line on GPIO 17 (BCM), the echo line on GPIO 27 (BCM) and a buzzer on GPIO 22 (BCM); the program must generate a 10 µs HIGH pulse on the trigger pin, use the library’s interrupt‑driven API to measure the echo time while correctly handling the driver’s 32‑bit tick wraparound, compute the distance in centimeters, and output the distance on the console every 100 ms, checking that the driver library initialization, GPIO mode configuration, and interrupt registration succeed and reporting clearly any sensor‑absent condition (timeout or no echo) or invalid reading (out‑of‑range), where valid readings are limited to 2 cm–400 cm, continuously activate the buzzer while the measured distance is less than 30 cm and turn it off when the distance rises to 30 cm or more, and ensure a clean shutdown on SIGINT that turns off the buzzer and calls the library’s API call() to release resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls a gate using a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 and an SG90 servo driven from GPIO18 (BCM) with hardware PWM, logging every event with a timestamp to a file named gate_log.txt; the program must perform full bare‑metal I2C initialization for the VL53L1X including a software reset, waiting for boot, starting ranging and reading the 16‑bit distance, automatically open the gate when an object is detected within 20 cm and close it when the path is clear, handle I2C communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions gracefully with retry logic, respond to remote‑control commands via the driver’s v2 callback API using the calls force_open, force_close and status_request, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using a falling‑edge interrupt on the echo pin over the GPIO bus, configuring TRIG on GPIO 23 (physical pin 16, BCM, output, initially LOW) and ECHO on GPIO 24 (physical pin 18, BCM, input, pull‑down) while noting in a comment that the ECHO line is 5 V and must be level‑shifted or divided for the Pi’s 3.3 V tolerance; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse every 200 ms (5 Hz sampling), register an alert callback that captures both rising and falling edge timestamps in microseconds, compute the pulse duration as falling_tick minus rising_tick while handling the driver’s 32‑bit tick wraparound (~72 min), reject any measured pulse width below 100 µs (noise) or above 30 000 µs (timeout/no object) and log such rejections as warnings, treat the absence of a valid echo within 60 ms of triggering as a timeout warning, and for each valid reading log the distance with an ISO 8601 timestamp to both stdout and an append‑mode file named distance_log.txt, flushing after each write; the program must initialize the driver library with full error checking, printing a diagnostic and exiting with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the log file, releasing GPIO resources via the library’s API call, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over the I2C bus, samples the sensor every 100 ms, computes the corresponding flow rate, and drives a PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering) using hardware PWM at a frequency of 25 kHz, while logging each measurement to a file named flow_log.txt in the format “timestamp,pressure_Pa\n”; the program must include robust handling of I2C communication failures by logging errors to stderr without crashing, and must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning off the fan, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW pressure sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second using the sensor’s API call, and logs each reading to a file named environmental_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C” by converting the current time with localtime_r; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, and on any failure write a timestamped error message to both stderr and the log file while continuing the loop, flush the log file after each write, and handle graceful termination on SIGINT by setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, then closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup call before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over the I2C bus, using a default sampling interval of 1000 ms that can be overridden with a command‑line argument, and prints each reading to the console with a timestamp; each reading must consist of exactly nine bytes – pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC‑8, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC‑8, scale‑factor MSB, scale‑factor LSB, scale‑factor CRC‑8 – and the program must verify the CRC‑8 for the pressure, temperature, and scale‑factor words, handle I2C failures robustly by detecting sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, emit a clear diagnostic message and exit if the sensor is not connected, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the program terminates with exit code 0 on those signals while still exiting with an error code on unrecoverable I2C errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus (bus 1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and then logging the results to stdout once every second; the implementation must open the I2C bus, verify successful driver initialization, perform a 9‑byte read that contains pressure, temperature and their respective scale factors, validate the CRC‑8 on each 3‑byte word using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle any CRC mismatch, sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions on every read/write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit kernel that periodically reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor attached via I2C on bus 1, with SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); the program must wait at least 20 ms after initiating a 14‑bit temperature and humidity conversion before reading the result, then log the values to the console every 5 seconds in the format “Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %”, while checking the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read() and write() call, handling the case where the sensor is absent (device file cannot be opened or no ACK is received) and, on any read failure, printing an error message to stderr and continuing the loop, and finally installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C file descriptor before exiting, noting that the DRDYn pin is not connected and the fixed delay must be relied upon for conversion timing.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads temperature from a Silicon Labs Si7051 temperature sensor connected via I2C on bus 1, using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), logging the measured temperature in degrees Celsius to the console every 5 seconds, with robust handling of I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the absolute pressure from a Melexis MLX90833 sensor over the I2C bus, logging the pressure value to the console together with a timestamp every 500 ms; the program must verify that all driver initialization steps succeed and must check the result of every I2C read and write operation, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that on any exit path all resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and pressure from a TDK ICP‑10101 barometric pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting 7 ms, then reading the results in a loop that repeats every 5 seconds; each successful read must be printed to stdout with an ISO‑8601 timestamp such as “2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa”, while every I2C driver call’s return value must be checked and a sensor‑absent condition detected when a read returns a negative value or all bytes match the documented default, logging an error message to stderr without terminating the program; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup call on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD‑to‑digital converter over SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 (GPIO8) at 1 MHz, operates the device in 3‑wire RTD mode with the bias voltage enabled, checks the fault status register on each read, computes the temperature using the Callendar‑Van Dusen equation, and logs the results every 5 seconds to a file named rtd_log.csv containing a timestamp and the temperature; the program must include robust error handling that logs SPI communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and any read errors without crashing, and it must perform a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature, humidity and pressure from a BME280 sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL, device file /dev/i2c-1) using the documented I2C address, verifies that the BME280 chip ID matches the documented value during initialization, and then logs a line to a file named bme280_log.csv every five seconds containing a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, the temperature in degrees Celsius, the relative humidity in percent, and the pressure in hectopascals; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all file descriptors and file pointers are cleanly released on any exit path, including when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, employing the library's API call for I2C communication and the library's API call for a hardware timer that triggers every 50 ms; each reading must be stored in a circular buffer sized to hold timestamped pressure values for the last 60 seconds, from which a rolling average is computed, and if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from that average the program shall assert an active‑HIGH alert on GPIO24, logging the alert to stderr, while also logging any I2C failures or sensor absence with robust error handling; the sampling loop must use the library's API call for the 50 ms timer, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release resources by closing the I2C interface, resetting GPIO24, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.
