prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor by counting its pulses on the GPIO bus, using GPIO18 (physical pin 12) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, counting only rising edges and assuming one pulse per revolution; the program must calculate the RPM over a 1‑second interval, protect the pulse counter with a pthread mutex shared between the interrupt service routine and the main thread, log each RPM value together with a timestamp to rpm_log.txt in append mode flushing the file immediately, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by terminating the driver library, closing the log file, and destroying the mutex, while also handling the case of a missing sensor by logging 0.00 RPM when no pulses are detected.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt, and triggers an LED connected to GPIO17 whenever the infrared reading exceeds a threshold of 2000; the implementation must robustly handle I2C errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and must clean up all resources—including the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and the log file—on every exit path, also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while avoiding any use of deprecated driver libraries or driver library components.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that samples the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier connected via GPIO, using the OUT pin (audio signal) on GPIO17 as an input and the GAIN select pin on GPIO18 as an output (set GPIO18 LOW to select 60 dB gain), polls the digital input every 10 ms to rapidly detect rising edges that indicate peak sound events, logs each detected event to a file named audio_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL” where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge, prints a startup message, and runs indefinitely until interrupted, while handling all driver library initialization and I/O errors robustly by checking the return value of every API call and ensuring clean release of all driver library resources on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the flow rate of a microfluidic drug delivery system using a Sensirion SLF3S‑4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected to I2C bus 1, reading the sensor every 1000 ms by retrieving three bytes (a two‑byte MSB‑first raw value followed by a CRC‑8 byte that must be validated with the documented polynomial and initial value), logging each successful measurement to a CSV file named flow_log.csv in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min” with the file opened once at startup in append mode, kept open, and flushed after each write; the program must check driver initialization, I2C open, write, and read operations, log any I2C read/write failures to stderr and attempt recovery on the next loop iteration, log a CRC failure as an error and skip that reading, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Honeywell MICS‑VZ‑89TE VOC sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the sensor data, computes an indoor air quality (IAQ) index, and logs a timestamped line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named air_quality_log.csv containing the IAQ value together with TVOC in ppb and eCO₂ in ppm; the implementation must check every I2C read and write return value, detect and handle conditions where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error without crashing, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt gracefully closes the I2C interface, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line wired to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) as an input with the consumer label “ttp223_tamper”, polling the line every 100 ms based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC; the program must detect when the TTP223B output, which is HIGH while touched and LOW when released, remains continuously HIGH for more than 5 seconds, then print a single intrusion alert to stdout for that touch event and reset the timer when the sensor is released so that alerts are not repeated for the same touch, while checking every library call for failure and printing strerror(errno) on error, and if a sensor read fails mid‑loop printing an error and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE after performing cleanup; the cleanup routine must also be invoked on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM to gracefully release the line and close the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples audio from an InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone over the I2S bus using the Linux ALSA subsystem (e.g., /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c) and writes the 16‑bit PCM samples to a raw file named audio_capture.pcm, while driving the L/R channel‑select line on GPIO 17 (BCM) to select the left channel, and includes robust handling of I2S initialization failures, data acquisition errors, and file I/O problems together with proper resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving a SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator with IR photodiode) connected via GPIO, reading the digital output (DO) on GPIO4 (BCM) every 50 ms and applying a 50 ms software debounce, and when the sensor output goes LOW indicating a flame, immediately start a hardware PWM signal at 100 Hz on GPIO18 (BCM) to drive a cooling fan, logging each event to a file named flame_log.txt with ISO‑8601 timestamps for system start, flame detection, flame end, and program shutdown; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, check the result of every GPIO read, detect a sensor‑absent condition by timing out if no valid reading is obtained, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly stop the PWM, reset the GPIO pins, terminate the driver library, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, using a hardware frame trigger on GPIO23 (BCM) and a data‑ready interrupt on GPIO24 (BCM) to capture range‑Doppler heatmap frames at a 100 ms period; the sensor is pre‑configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range‑Doppler data, with a configuration struct that records a start frequency of 77 GHz, end frequency of 79 GHz, 64 chirps and 256 samples, and each frame requires a full‑duplex SPI transfer of 32 768 bytes of heatmap data, which must be logged to a binary file whose header contains the documented magic number 4144, an 8‑byte timestamp and the configuration struct, followed by per‑frame timestamps and frame numbers, while checking all return codes, handling any memory allocation failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program gracefully closes the SPI device, releases the GPIO pins and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output of a KY‑026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO20 (BCM) on the GPIO bus every 100 ms, detects when the sensor state changes between flame detected and flame cleared, and appends a line to a file named flame_log.txt containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the new state only on each transition; the implementation must verify the success of every driver call and every file‑I/O operation, explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Texas Instruments OPT3001 Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous conversion mode with automatic full‑scale range, reads lux values approximately every 100 ms conversion time, and appends each reading to a file named light_data.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the implementation must robustly handle I2C transaction failures and sensor‑absent conditions by retrying or logging errors without crashing, and must perform a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by releasing the I2C bus handle, any driver resources, and closing all open file handles on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the SainSmart IR Flame Detection Sensor Module over the GPIO bus, requesting the flame sensor DOUT line as an input with a pulled‑up bias on GPIO line 17 (BCM, active‑low) using the driver library v2 API calls, and logs the status to the console once every second; each log entry must be formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” followed by “Flame Detected: YES” when the sensor value is 0 or “Flame Detected: NO” when the value is 1, while checking every driver library call and syscall for errors and printing clear error messages to stderr; the program must install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to break the main loop, and on cleanup it must release the line request, close the chip, and free all configuration and settings objects, and it must be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_detect flame_detect.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the Keywish KY‑033 3‑Way Tracing Sensor over GPIO, using GPIO17 (BCM) for the left output, GPIO18 (BCM) for the center output, and GPIO27 (BCM) for the right output, polling each pin every 50 ms with usleep(50000), printing the current states to the console in the format “Left: %d, Center: %d, Right: %d”, checking the return value of every library API call and, on any failure, printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads a TTP226 8‑channel digital touch sensor configured for direct GPIO output and logs each channel’s state, using the GPIO bus and connecting OUT1‑OUT8 to BCM GPIO pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 respectively; the program must poll the eight lines every 100 ms and print to the console a timestamped line showing the binary state (0 or 1) of each channel, must check the return values of all driver calls for opening the chip, requesting the lines and reading their values and print descriptive error messages to stderr when any call fails, must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown, and must ensure that all resources such as line handles and the chip are properly released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a TTP226 8-channel digital touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, configuring the eight sensor output pins OUT1‑OUT8 as Broadcom GPIO 2‑9 inputs with pull‑down resistors, initializing the driver library and checking the return value to abort with an error message if initialization fails, then entering a loop that calls the library’s API function with a 100 000‑microsecond (100 ms) sampling interval, validating the return of each API call and aborting with a diagnostic on any failure, printing to the console for each sample a line such as “[+1234 ms] CH1=0 CH2=1 … CH8=0”, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the loop can exit cleanly and the library’s API call is always invoked during shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads two Texas Instruments TMAG5110 Hall‑Effect Latch sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 OUT wired to BCM GPIO4 and sensor 2 OUT wired to BCM GPIO5, and logs each sensor’s state as HIGH or LOW to the console every 500 ms; the implementation must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the GPIO pins are configured in the proper mode, treat the sensor outputs as open‑drain with external pull‑up resistors (so an unasserted output reads HIGH and a magnet‑detected assertion reads LOW), handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform clean resource release and ensure the driver library is terminated on all exit paths, and be compiled with the command `gcc -Wall -o hall_effect hall_effect.c -lthe driver library -lrt`.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected via the GPIO bus, with the sensor’s digital output (DO) wired to GPIO17 (Broadcom pin 17, physical pin 11) configured as an input with an internal pull‑up, and polls the line every 100 ms to detect a falling‑edge event (the transition from HIGH to LOW, since the sensor is active‑low: LOW indicates a flame); on each detected falling edge the program must print “FLAME DETECTED” to the console and append a timestamped “FLAME DETECTED” line to a file named flame_log.txt opened in append mode with an immediate flush, while ensuring that duplicate alerts are not generated while the line remains low; every driver library call and file operation must be checked for errors, and the code must handle the situation where the GPIO chip or the specific line is unavailable; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to perform graceful shutdown on all exit paths by releasing the GPIO line, closing the GPIO chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the GPIO bus to read an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module connected on BCM pins 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 (OUT1‑OUT8) and drives an 8‑bit binary counter on GPIO 17 through GPIO 24 (bit 0 on 17, bit 7 on 24), polling the sensor lines every 10 ms after an initial 200 ms stabilization delay; on each rising edge (idle 0 V to touched 3.3 V) the program must increment the counter, wrapping from 255 to 0, immediately update the eight output pins via the driver’s bulk/config API calls, and log the event to a file named touch_log.txt in append mode using an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp “YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1‑8>, Counter: <0‑255>” while also printing to stdout “Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>”, checking every driver call, file open and I/O operation and reporting errors with strerror(errno); if any line request fails the program must clean up all previously acquired resources and exit non‑zero, if a driver API call fails it must print the error and exit non‑zero, if a sensor read returns an error it must log the error to stderr and skip that channel for the iteration, if an output write fails it must log the error to stderr but continue, and if opening the log file fails it must warn on stderr yet keep stdout output functional; finally the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all driver resources, closing the chip and exiting with status 0, and it must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that polls four Keywish KY-033 4‑Way Infrared Tracking Module sensors connected via GPIO—sensor 1 on GPIO17 (BCM), sensor 2 on GPIO18 (BCM), sensor 3 on GPIO27 (BCM), and sensor 4 on GPIO22 (BCM)—every 100 ms, reading each active‑low output (0 indicates line or obstacle detected, 1 indicates no line), and appends a row to a timestamped CSV file named tracking_log.csv with columns timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,sensor3,sensor4, writing a header row if the file does not yet exist; the program must robustly check every initialization and read call, printing clear error messages to stderr and continuing when possible if a GPIO request or read fails, must use the modern driver library API calls for GPIO handling, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes and flushes the CSV file after each write to prevent data loss on abrupt termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors two Omron D7E‑5 tilt sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM, physical pin 12), configuring both lines as inputs with an active‑low pull‑up (BiasPullUp) so that an unconnected sensor reads high and a tilt event pulls the line low; the program must poll both lines every 100 ms and use a 50 ms debounce window to detect edges, logging only transitions from inactive (1) to active (0) by appending a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Sensor X tilted\n” where X is 1 for GPIO17 and 2 for GPIO18, handling chip open failure, line request failure, and read errors by printing an error message to stderr and either exiting or continuing gracefully as appropriate, and installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that release all driver resources (chip and lines) and close the log file cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads reflectance data from two TCRT5000 IR obstacle‑avoidance sensor modules connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO27 (BCM), and drives an LED on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must poll both sensors every 100 ms, treat the sensors as active‑low (0 indicates an obstacle, 1 indicates clear), turn the LED high only when both sensors read 0, and log each sample to a file named obstacle_log.csv using the column order timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,led_state, flushing the file after every write; it must check the result of every driver library C‑API call, handle the situation where any API call is unavailable, verify that the log file opens successfully, and on receiving a SIGINT perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off, releasing all line resources, closing the chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples the analog output of a TDK InvenSense ICS‑40180 analog MEMS microphone connected to GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by polling the pin as a digital input at roughly 8 kHz (a 125 µs period) using the provided library’s API call, treats any HIGH reading as a sound‑peak event, prints a millisecond‑precision timestamp to stdout for each detected peak, and for each peak turns on an LED wired with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor on GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) for exactly 100 ms; the program must check the return value of every library API call and report any errors to stderr, employ a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to catch SIGINT, and on receiving that signal cleanly stop the sampling loop, ensure the LED is turned OFF, and invoke the library’s shutdown API call, while never calling any library functions directly from within the signal handler.

/*
 * FXOS8700 accelerometer + magnetometer reader for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   FXOS8700 SDA  -> GPIO2  (BCM pin 3, I2C bus 1 SDA)
 *   FXOS8700 SCL  -> GPIO3  (BCM pin 5, I2C bus 1 SCL)
 *   FXOS8700 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   FXOS8700 GND  -> GND
 *
 * The FXOS8700 is a 12-lead breakout with a 12-byte combined block
 * returned on every read.  The block layout is:
 *
 *   [0..5]  accel X/Y/Z (14-bit left-aligned, 2-bit resolution)
 *   [6..11] mag X/Y/Z (16-bit, 2's complement)
 *   [12]   reserved / 0
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o fxos8700 fxos8700.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./fxos8700
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

/* ---- FXOS8700 constants (from the Adafruit breakout datasheet) ---- */
#define FXOS8700_ADDR        0x60
#define FXOS8700_REG_ID      0x00
#define FXOS8700_REG_CTRL    0x01
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XL  0x08
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XH  0x0A
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XL_H 0x0B
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XH_H 0x0D
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZL  0x0C
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZL_H 0x0E
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_YL  0x0F
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_YL_H 0x11
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZM  0x12
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZM_H 0x14

#define FXOS8700_ID_VALUE    0x87

/*
 * CTRL register bits (16-bit, big-endian on the wire):
 *   [15]   ODR[14:12]  -> 000 -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [11:10]  ODR[9:8]   -> 10  -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [7:6]   ODR[5:4]   -> 00  -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [3:2]   ODR[1:0]   -> 10  -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [1]    ODR[0]      -> 0   -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [15:12] reserved
 *   [11:10] MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR
 *   [3:2]   NDR
 *   [1:0]   NCLR
 *   [11]    reserved
 *   [10]   MHDR
 *   [9:8]   NHDR
 *   [7:6]   NCLR
 *   [5:4]   MNDR

/*
 * FXOS8700 accelerometer + magnetometer reader for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   FXOS8700 SDA  -> GPIO2  (BCM pin 3, I2C bus 1 SDA)
 *   FXOS8700 SCL  -> GPIO3  (BCM pin 5, I2C bus 1 SCL)
 *   FXOS8700 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   FXOS8700 GND  -> GND
 *
 * The FXOS8700 is a 12-lead breakout with a 12-byte combined block
 * returned on every read.  The block layout is:
 *
 *   [0..5]  accel X/Y/Z (14-bit left-aligned, 2-bit resolution)
 *   [6..11] mag X/Y/Z (16-bit, 2's complement)
 *   [12]   reserved / 0
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o fxos8700 fxos8700.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./fxos8700
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

/* ---- FXOS8700 constants (from the Adafruit breakout datasheet) ---- */
#define FXOS8700_ADDR        0x60
#define FXOS8700_REG_ID      0x00
#define FXOS8700_REG_CTRL    0x01
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XL  0x08
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XH  0x0A
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XL_H 0x0B
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_XH_H 0x0D
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZL  0x0C
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZL_H 0x0E
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_YL  0x0F
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_YL_H 0x11
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZM  0x12
#define FXOS8700_REG_OUT_ZM_H 0x14

#define FXOS8700_ID_VALUE    0x87

/*
 * CTRL register bits (16-bit, big-endian on the wire):
 *   [15]   ODR[14:12]  -> 000 -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [11:10]  ODR[9:8]   -> 10  -> 62.5 Hz
 *   [7:6]   ODR[5:4]   -> 00  -> 62.5 Hz

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the digital OUT line of a KY‑038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) over successive 5‑second windows, sampling the pin every 1 ms; after each 5‑second window the program must print to stdout a timestamped line either “ALERT” if the count of high readings exceeds a user‑defined threshold or a status line otherwise, then pause for 1 second before starting the next window, accepting a single command‑line argument that is an integer threshold of minimum high‑readings per window and rejecting any non‑numeric or non‑positive values with a clear error printed to stderr; every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for failure and any error reported to stderr; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by terminating the driver usage and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that controls two 12 V electromagnetic door locks via TIP120‑driven 5 V active‑HIGH relay modules on the GPIO bus, using GPIO17 (BCM) for Door A and GPIO27 (BCM) for Door B, both initialized as outputs with a default LOW state that keeps the locks energized/closed and a HIGH level that de‑energizes the relay to unlock the door for exactly 5 seconds; at program start and after each successful entry the application must generate a random six‑digit security code in the range 100000‑999999, print it to stdout, then read user input from stdin, handling non‑numeric input by clearing the buffer and re‑prompting, compare the entered code to the generated one, and on a match log a CSV line “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN” to a file named access_log.txt, while printing “Access denied” and continuing on a mismatch; every driver call that opens the chip, gets a line, or requests a line as well as the file open must be checked, with meaningful error messages sent to stderr and a non‑zero exit on any initialization failure; the program must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on termination it must set both GPIO outputs to LOW (locking the doors), release all driver resources and close any open file handles; the source must compile with gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3) with the ADDR pin tied to GND, waits up to the maximum 180 ms conversion time, and logs a reading every 5 seconds to a file named light_log.txt using the format “Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>”, while handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent (for example failing to open the bus or read bytes), and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) signal.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads tilt data from an MPU‑6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, computes roll and pitch, prints both values to the console each cycle, and appends a line to a file named tilt_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp (YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS), roll and pitch; the program must check that the I2C bus opens successfully, that the sensor is initialized, and that each read operation succeeds, logging any read error and continuing without crashing; an LED connected to GPIO21 (BCM numbering) shall be turned on whenever the absolute value of roll exceeds 45 degrees or the absolute value of pitch exceeds 45 degrees and turned off otherwise, and on receipt of a SIGINT (Ctrl +C) the program must clean up by turning off the LED, closing the I2C handle and terminating the driver library, while using the driver library for all sensor interactions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates with a Si1145 optical biometric sensor (register‑compatible with the Si1182‑A‑GM) over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented 8‑bit address, reads ambient light and proximity values every 100 ms, and on each successful read appends a line to biometric_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,AmbientLight:XXXX,Proximity:XXXX”; if a read fails the program must retry up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts, and if the proximity value exceeds 100 the program must set GPIO17 (BCM numbering) high to turn on a presence LED, otherwise keep it low, while using only modern Linux APIs such as open, ioctl, read/write and signal handling; the program must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully close the I2C file descriptor, close the log file, and turn off the LED before exiting.
pinned_library: libgpiod for GPIO, Linux i2c-dev interface for I2C

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch controller on I2C bus 1 to read touch status every 10 ms, debounces touch events with a 100 ms delay, and toggles a 5 V relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) each time electrode 0 is touched, initializing GPIO17 to a default LOW state; the program must check every initialization step and every I2C operation for errors, log all I2C, GPIO, and configuration errors with timestamps to a file named touch_relay.log, and on any failure log the error and exit gracefully, while also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to cleanly close the I2C interface, release the GPIO pin, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors a KY-026 flame sensor module whose digital output (active‑low) is connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and, when three consecutive reads spaced 50 ms apart all indicate a LOW level, logs a timestamp and the text “Flame Detected” to a file named flame_log.txt, then activates a buzzer on GPIO18 (BCM) and an LED on GPIO23 (BCM) for as long as the sensor remains LOW, turning both off when the flame condition clears; the implementation must include robust error handling for every GPIO operation, must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully release the GPIO lines and close the log file, and must ensure that all resources are released on any error exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives a pneumatic dispensing system using two 12 V push‑pull solenoids controlled through TIP120 Darlington transistors, with solenoid 1 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and solenoid 2 to GPIO27 (BCM); the program must dispense every 5 seconds in a continuous loop, activating solenoid 1 for the first half of a total 1000 ms dispense interval, then solenoid 2 for the remaining half, deactivating both afterwards, using the library’s call() function for timing, while logging each dispense event to a file named dispense_log.txt that records the timestamp, the solenoid pins, and the duration in milliseconds; it must handle driver library initialization failure gracefully by printing an error to stderr and exiting, ensure every function returns 0 on success and non‑zero on failure with main checking these return values and printing appropriate error messages to stderr, handle file open failures similarly, register a SIGINT handler that on Ctrl +C gracefully deactivates both solenoids, terminates the driver library, and exits, and the source must compile with the driver library linked via the -lthe driver library flag.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a self‑balancing robot using PID‑controlled motors and obstacle‑avoidance from a simulated ultrasonic sensor, driving two DC motors through an L298N dual H‑bridge with Motor A forward on GPIO17 (BCM), Motor A backward on GPIO18 (BCM), Motor B forward on GPIO22 (BCM), Motor B backward on GPIO23 (BCM), ENA on GPIO24 (BCM) and ENB on GPIO25 (BCM) which must be held HIGH to enable PWM control, running the PID control loop every 50 ms, generating a log file named balance_log.txt with columns timestamp (YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS), tilt_error, distance, motor_a_speed and motor_b_speed, where the simulated tilt error is a random float between –10.0 and 10.0 degrees and the simulated ultrasonic distance sensor returns a random value between 2.0 and 400.0 cm, and if the distance falls below 20 cm the robot must reverse both motors at 50 % speed for obstacle avoidance while clamping all motor speeds to ±255, handling driver library initialization failure by printing an error and returning 1, handling log file open failure by printing an error, terminating the driver library and returning 1, logging and skipping any invalid motor character, and on SIGINT cleanly stopping the motors, closing the log file and terminating the driver library gracefully, using only the driver library functions and no deprecated API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7, BCM numbering) and toggles a 5 V relay attached to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM) each time a touch is detected, using the sensor’s logic‑HIGH output to indicate a touch, applying an internal or external pull‑down as needed, enforcing a debounce delay of at least 50 ms after each detection, and ensuring that the relay is active‑high (energized when GPIO17 is HIGH); the implementation must verify successful initialization of the GPIO driver and each GPIO operation, gracefully handle conditions such as the sensor being absent or bus errors, and include robust cleanup that releases all resources on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while running indefinitely until terminated with Ctrl‑C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures audio using ALSA at an 8000 Hz sample rate, 16‑bit signed little‑endian, mono, with a period size of 1024 frames on the device named “default”, computes the RMS amplitude of each buffer and, every 10 ms, maps that amplitude non‑linearly to a common‑cathode RGB LED’s color by driving the red channel on GPIO17 (BCM), green on GPIO18 (BCM) and blue on GPIO27 (BCM) with software PWM through the driver library’s API, using current‑limiting resistors; the program must print status messages to stdout and errors to stderr, check the result of every driver library and ALSA call, recover from buffer overruns (EPIPE) with snd_pcm_prepare and from suspended state (ESTRPIPE) with snd_pcm_resume, accept an optional positive command‑line argument that scales sensitivity (default 1.0), gate all ALSA‑related code behind an ALSA_AVAILABLE compile‑time macro and, when ALSA is not available, simulate audio input with a sine‑wave amplitude so the mood light still cycles through colors, and finally install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly release all resources—including the driver library, ALSA handles and any allocated memory—ensuring no leaks on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on the I2C bus, reading acceleration at a 10 Hz interval (every 100 ms) and configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, high‑resolution 12‑bit left‑justified mode with a 100 Hz output data rate, supporting only a single sensor; the program must accept optional command‑line arguments “‑a” for the I2C address in hex and “‑t” for a threshold in g (default 2.0 g, must be > 0), validate that the address falls within the documented range, and on any axis exceeding the threshold log a line containing a timestamp and the three axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log before invoking “sudo shutdown -h now”; it must handle I2C open or configuration errors by performing cleanup (closing the bus and terminating the driver library) and exiting with code 0 in non‑hardware environments, handle sensor read errors by returning zeros and continuing, use the library’s API calls for I2C operations and single‑byte register writes (which return 0 on success), and install a SIGINT handler that gracefully terminates by closing I2C and shutting down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements an autonomous line‑following robot using a SunFounder 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected on the GPIO bus, with the left sensor wired to GPIO4 (BCM), the center sensor to GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor to GPIO27 (BCM) and an active‑high alert LED/buzzer on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must poll the three sensor pins every 10 ms, log each reading (left, center, right) into a circular buffer of size five, check all driver library initialization and line‑request return values and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, drive the alert pin HIGH for 2 seconds when the center sensor reports “no line” (logic 1) for five consecutive readings, otherwise move forward when the center detects a line (logic 0), turn left when the left sensor detects a line, turn right when the right sensor detects a line, and stop when all sensors read “no line”, using placeholder motor control functions, and ensure that on any exit path triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources are cleanly released.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with BCM numbering to control a KY‑019 relay module connected to GPIO 18, listening on TCP port 5000 for case‑insensitive commands “ON” and “OFF” (trailing whitespace must be ignored), invoking the library’s API call to switch the relay and logging every activation, deactivation, and any invalid‑command event with a timestamp to a file named relay_log.txt; the implementation must include comprehensive error handling for all socket operations (creation, bind, listen, accept, and read) as well as for GPIO initialization, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that gracefully shut down the library’s API call, close the sockets and the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control a hobby servo acting as a door‑lock actuator based on two momentary push‑buttons, with the servo connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18), the lock button to GPIO 21 (BCM) and the unlock button to GPIO 22 (BCM), both buttons wired to ground when pressed and therefore requiring internal pull‑up resistors to be enabled; the program must poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to keep CPU usage low, implement debouncing by waiting for the button release plus a short delay so that a single press is not registered multiple times, drive the library’s API call() with a 2000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 21 button is pressed to lock, a 1000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 22 button is pressed to unlock, and output status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events, verify that the API call() returns success for both pulse‑width commands and exit with an error message on failure, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the servo by sending a pulse width of 0, calls the API call() one final time, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to control a servo motor on BCM GPIO17 and read a PIR sensor on BCM GPIO4, listening for TCP connections on port 5000; the program must accept commands of the form “the library's API call <angle>” where <angle> is 0‑180 and generate a software PWM signal at 50 Hz with a 1‑2 ms pulse width to position the servo, and also respond to the command “PIR” by sending back “PIR:0” or “PIR:1” over the socket, while logging all events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps, checking the result of every driver library call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation and, if GPIO initialization fails, logging the error and exiting with a non‑zero status; the code must include <stdarg.h> for variadic functions so it compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes the socket and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C1 (GPIO2 =SDA, GPIO3 =SCL) using the documented address, waiting at least 120 ms after each trigger before reading the 2‑byte lux result and sampling every 2 seconds, logs a timestamp and the lux value to grow_log.txt, and drives a grow‑light relay on GPIO23 (BCM) so that the relay is activated when the lux reading falls below 150 and deactivated when it is 150 or above, while implementing robust error handling that checks the return codes of every I2C call and of file operations, logs any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions and simply retries on the next cycle, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the program cleanly releases all resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, deactivating the relay, and invoking the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors weight using a TAL220B load cell with an HX711 amplifier over a bit‑banged GPIO bus, reading HX711 DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and HX711 SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and drives a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22); the program must perform a startup tare by averaging ten 24‑bit two’s‑complement readings (obtained by waiting for DOUT to go LOW, clocking out 24 bits MSB‑first, then one extra clock pulse to select Channel A gain 128), then in the main loop poll the weight every 500 ms, averaging five readings per measurement cycle, apply an optional scale factor, and if the measured weight exceeds a threshold (default 1000 grams, overridable with a --threshold <grams> command‑line argument) activate the solenoid lock by setting GPIO25 HIGH for 200 ms before returning it LOW; each HX711 read must check that DOUT goes LOW within 1 second, logging an error via syslog and retrying up to three times before exiting, and every driver call must be verified for errors; the program should accept optional --scale <factor> and --duration <ms> arguments, log informational and error messages through syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and chips, closes syslog, and ensures the solenoid is set LOW before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that controls a relay module attached to the GPIO bus on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) by subscribing to the MQTT topic home/lights/control with QoS 0, connecting to a broker at localhost port 1883 using client ID relay_controller_1 and a clean session, maintaining a 60‑second keep‑alive, and on successful connect logging the event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay) and subscribing to the topic; the program must initialize the GPIO driver, configure GPIO17 as an output and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup, then in the main thread run the MQTT client loop, handling incoming payloads as NUL‑terminated strings where the exact values “ON” set GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and “OFF” set it LOW (relay de‑energized), logging any empty or invalid payload as an error (syslog LOG_ERR) without changing the relay state, and for every connection, subscription, disconnection, or error event logging the details to syslog, checking all return codes from the driver and MQTT client and reporting failures via syslog while never exiting on transient MQTT errors; on loop errors or unexpected disconnects the program must wait five seconds before attempting to reconnect, and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the MQTT client, clean up the driver library, call the library cleanup function, and close the syslog; the source should be compiled with gcc using optimization level 2 and all warnings enabled, producing an executable named relay_controller.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that moves five hobby servos connected to the GPIO bus to predefined positions by generating a 50 Hz PWM signal (20 ms period) on BCM GPIO 7 for Servo 1, BCM GPIO 8 for Servo 2, BCM GPIO 9 for Servo 3, BCM GPIO 10 for Servo 4, and BCM GPIO 11 for Servo 5, holding each pulse for three seconds; the program must initialize the driver library and verify the return code before use, then output pulse widths constrained between 500 µs and 2500 µs with target values of 1000 µs, 1500 µs, 2000 µs, 500 µs, and 2500 µs respectively for the five servos, and finally cleanly stop the PWM and release all library resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements closed‑loop DC motor speed control for a miniature vehicle using quadrature encoders, driving two DC motors through a DRV8833 H‑bridge on the GPIO bus with PWM and digital signals; use GPIO 17 (BCM) as Motor A PWM (IN1), GPIO 18 as Motor A direction (IN2), GPIO 22 as Motor B PWM (IN3), GPIO 23 as Motor B direction (IN4), read Encoder A phase A on GPIO 4, Encoder A phase B on GPIO 5, Encoder B phase A on GPIO 6, and Encoder B phase B on GPIO 12, run a PI control loop every 100 ms with a 10 kHz PWM frequency, assume 64 ticks per revolution with a single count per rising edge and a 1:1 encoder‑to‑output‑shaft ratio, target 50 RPM for both motors, drive each motor by holding one input pin high and PWM‑modulating the other for forward motion, clamp the PWM duty cycle to the range 0‑255 and implement anti‑windup clamping in the controller, maintain encoder tick counters with atomic operations, detect an encoder stall when zero ticks are observed for more than 2 seconds and print a warning, print the motor RPM and PWM duty cycle each control iteration, check the driver library initialization and ISR registration calls and exit cleanly on any failure, and handle SIGINT by stopping the motors and releasing all resources, ensuring the code compiles cleanly with ‑Wall.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors ambient light using a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) and controls a 12 V LED strip through a relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM, active‑high), polling the sensor every 5 seconds and waiting at least 180 ms after issuing the mode command before reading, logging each sensor reading and any relay state change to a file named chicken_coop_log.txt in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Lux = XXX, Relay = ON/OFF”, activating the relay at dusk when lux falls below 50 and deactivating it at dawn when lux rises above 200 with hysteresis to avoid rapid toggling, implementing comprehensive error handling for driver initialization, I2C communication and file I/O such that any sensor non‑response is logged and the relay is safely turned off, and ensuring that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin and the log file—are cleanly released on every exit path, including graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO bus to read a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7) as an input and control a 5 V relay on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) as an output, implementing a touch‑toggled relay with debouncing: each valid touch detection must toggle the relay state only when the sensor reads HIGH both before and after a 50 ms debounce stabilization delay, then wait for the sensor to return LOW before allowing the next toggle (edge detection on touch‑release), with the main loop sleeping 10 ms between iterations; every relay state change must be logged to the console with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the new state (ON or OFF); the program must check the return value of every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call) and report any errors to stderr; a SIGINT handler must turn the relay OFF, release the driver library resources, and print an exit message; no MQTT or networking code is to be included.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors water flow using a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) and controls a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 (BCM) via the GPIO bus, implementing a 1‑second ISR debounce timeout on the flow‑sensor pin and sampling the pulse count every second; the program must protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex, log each liters‑per‑minute (LPM) reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to a file named water_flow.log, initialize the driver library and validate all return codes for each library API call, and if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non‑zero status; the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and must be driven LOW to shut off when the measured flow exceeds 5.0 LPM, reopening only when the flow drops below 4.5 LPM to provide a 0.5 L/min hysteresis, and the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, returning the solenoid to its safe open state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling the library’s cleanup API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4/5 (using the 40‑pin header) that lets a user adjust the angle of a hobby servo such as an SG90 via keyboard input, driving the servo on GPIO18 (BCM 18, physical pin 12) with hardware PWM on the GPIO bus at a 50 Hz frequency (20 ms period); the program must start the servo at 90° (1500 µs pulse width), increase the angle by 10° for each ‘+’ key and decrease by 10° for each ‘‑’ key, clamp the angle between 0° and 180° and ensure the computed pulse widths stay within the 500‑2500 µs range, print the current angle after every change, read keys in raw terminal mode so no Enter is required, use the library's API call() to set the pulse width (checking its return value and printing any error to stderr before exiting with a non‑zero status), and on receiving ‘q’ or a SIGINT must stop PWM pulses on GPIO18, invoke the library's API call() one final time, restore the terminal settings and properly save and restore the driver library state even on unexpected exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the RPM of a conveyor‑belt motor using an A3144 Hall‑effect sensor and a two‑pole magnet mounted on the motor shaft, connecting the sensor to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) with the internal pull‑up bias flag enabled; the program must use edge‑triggered event detection on the rising edge (the two‑pole magnet yields one pulse per revolution), apply a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double‑edge noise, count pulses with a monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC), compute the motor RPM every 5 seconds, and after each interval write a line to motor_rpm.log in CSV format containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the RPM value to two decimal places (flushed after every write) while also printing the current RPM to stdout; it must check the library’s API call return values, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status on any failure, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by stopping the main loop, releasing the GPIO line, closing the chip and the log file, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses a GPIO bus to read a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on BCM GPIO4 and drive a 5 V active‑HIGH relay on BCM GPIO17, polling the sensor every 50 ms and toggling the relay state on each rising edge of the touch; if the sensor remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds the program must force the relay OFF and ignore further toggles until the sensor is released, while checking the return value of the library's API call() and every the library's API call()/the library's API call()/the library's API call() call and, if the library's API call() returns PI_BAD_GPIO, logging the error and exiting; SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers should set a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, after which main() must release the relay (set OFF) and call the library's API call() for cleanup, with all cleanup performed outside the signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements closed‑loop proportional solenoid valve flow control using an ASCO RedHat 8210 series proportional solenoid valve and a YF‑S201 flow sensor on a GPIO bus with hardware PWM and interrupt‑driven pulse counting; the valve PWM must be generated on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), the valve enable/direction line on GPIO 23 (BCM, active‑high) which should be driven high at startup, and the flow sensor must be connected to GPIO 24 (BCM) with an interrupt on each rising edge, sampling the flow rate every 100 ms, applying a proportional controller with Kp = 1.0 to compute a PWM duty cycle in the range 0‑255 (clamped to that range) based on a target flow rate supplied as a command‑line argument “-t” in L/min (the program must validate this argument and exit with an error if it is missing or invalid), logging on each control iteration a line containing timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to a local file named flow_log.csv; the program must check initialization of the driver library, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file opening, exiting with a diagnostic message on any failure, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that sets the PWM duty cycle to zero, drives GPIO 23 low, closes the CSV file, and cleanly terminates the driver library, while never using any network logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a two‑factor door access control using two YLI YM‑180 electromagnetic lock actuators and an RFID reader on SPI channel 0 at 100 kHz, where the locks are wired to GPIO 17 (Lock 1) and GPIO 27 (Lock 2) in BCM numbering and the button is on GPIO 22 (active‑low with internal pull‑up and a 50 ms debounce, also BCM); the program must poll the RFID reader in a non‑blocking loop using the library's API call(), verify a valid 10‑byte tag (the documented value), then require a button press before disengaging both locks by driving their GPIO pins LOW for exactly 5 seconds and then re‑engaging them HIGH, while logging every access attempt—including successful entry, invalid tag, RFID read failure, and button press without a valid tag—with ISO‑8601 timestamps to /var/log/door_access.log; it must treat an all‑zero 10‑byte SPI response as “no tag present” rather than an error, handle SPI read failures gracefully without crashing, and perform error handling by checking the library's API call() four times and the file open operation, and finally install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI interface, forces both locks to the engaged (HIGH) state, closes the log file, and calls the library's API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements PID speed control for two L298N‑driven DC motors equipped with quadrature encoders, using the GPIO bus; the program must drive Motor 1 ENA on GPIO 23 (BCM), Motor 1 IN1 on GPIO 24 (BCM), Motor 1 IN2 on GPIO 25 (BCM), Motor 2 ENB on GPIO 12 (BCM), Motor 2 IN3 on GPIO 16 (BCM), Motor 2 IN4 on GPIO 20 (BCM), read Encoder 1 A on GPIO 5 (BCM) and Encoder 1 B on GPIO 6 (BCM), and read Encoder 2 A on GPIO 26 (BCM) and Encoder 2 B on GPIO 19 (BCM), with a PID sample time of 100 ms and a software PWM fixed at about 100 Hz, logging motor speeds in RPM, the P, I, and D components, and the PID output to a file named motor_log.csv that includes a header row and is flushed after each write; the code must verify all driver calls for opening the chip, requesting lines, and setting edge events, check file operations, and handle encoder read failures gracefully, use quadrature decoding by configuring BOTH_EDGES on the A pins and reading the B pin to determine direction, compute duty cycles proportional to the PID output, target a hard‑coded speed of 60 RPM for both motors, run encoder monitoring in separate threads protected by mutexes to keep encoder counts thread‑safe, and install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that stop the motors, release GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file, operating indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reading the touch status of all twelve electrodes every 50 ms, and drives a relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) so that any touched electrode sets the relay output HIGH and no electrodes touched sets it LOW, while every change of the relay state is appended with a timestamp to a text file named relay_log.txt; the program must perform a robust MPR121 initialization sequence that includes a soft reset, configuration of the filtering parameters, setting of touch and release thresholds for each of the twelve electrodes, and enabling run mode, and it must include comprehensive error handling that checks the initialization of the sensor driver, all I2C open, read and write operations, and gracefully handles cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, and it must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) signal to shut down the relay and close any I2C handles properly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a timed water distribution schedule for two Adafruit Solenoid Valves, Product ID 997, each driven through a relay module on the GPIO bus, with Valve 1’s relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) and Valve 2’s relay connected to GPIO 18 (BCM); the program must repeatedly activate Valve 1 for 500 ms then pause 5 seconds, activate Valve 2 for 1000 ms then pause 10 seconds, logging every activation event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named valve_log.txt, include robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization failures, line request failures, and file I/O errors, and install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that ensure clean release of all GPIO lines and closure of the log file on exit, while observing that each 12 V, 0.7 A valve is controlled only via its relay (GPIO HIGH = relay ON = valve OPEN, GPIO LOW = relay OFF = valve CLOSED) and the schedule repeats indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls a line‑following robot using a Keywish 3‑Way Infrared Tracking Sensor and two DC motors driven through an L298N motor driver, communicating over the GPIO / PWM bus; the left sensor must be read from GPIO4 (BCM), the middle sensor from GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor from GPIO27 (BCM), and the motor PWM signals must be output on GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24 and GPIO25 (BCM), with all three sensor inputs sampled every 10 ms and the PWM signals generated at a 1 kHz frequency, while the sensors provide active‑low digital signals and the control law requires that when the middle sensor is low the robot drives straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255, when only the left sensor is low the robot turns right by halving the left motor speed, when only the right sensor is low it turns left by halving the right motor speed, and when no sensor is low both motors are stopped; each control cycle must be logged to a file named trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states (0/1), and the left and right motor speeds, and the implementation must include robust error handling for initializing the driver library, opening the log file, and all GPIO operations, and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt stops both motors, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and ensures that all driver library API calls are properly released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads illuminance from a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1, observes a 180 ms measurement delay, and drives a relay connected to GPIO23 (BCM) to turn on a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150, logging each lux value and every relay state change with millisecond‑precision timestamps to a file named grow_log.txt; the program must handle I2C errors gracefully by logging any sensor detection or read failures and continuing operation without crashing, run indefinitely until a SIGINT is received, and on that signal cleanly release all resources by closing the I2C handle, turning off the relay, and terminating the driver library, using only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a door lock using the library's API call to drive a servo motor on the GPIO/PWM bus, with the servo connected to GPIO18 (BCM) and two push‑buttons connected to GPIO21 (BCM) for lock and GPIO22 (BCM) for unlock, both using pull‑up resistors and active‑low logic (reading 0 when pressed); the program must debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay, set the servo pulse width to 1000 µs (≈0°) when the lock button is pressed and to 2000 µs (≈180°) when the unlock button is pressed while respecting the API’s safe pulse‑width range of 500‑2500 µs, print status messages for each action, handle any initialization failures gracefully by printing an error message, and install a SIGINT signal handler that cleanly releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that generates a haptic feedback system by pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310‑101 vibration motors sequentially and repeatedly over the GPIO bus, driving motor 1 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for 200 ms, then motor 2 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for 300 ms, and looping this pattern indefinitely; the design must include robust error handling that checks every driver library call for line request failures and value write failures, as well as proper registration of signal handlers, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully release the GPIO lines and stop the motors by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths, while observing the constraint that the motors require 3 V at 60 mA typical and therefore must be driven through an external driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode rather than being connected directly to the GPIO pins.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a sound‑triggered alarm as a single executable with two selectable modes chosen by a command‑line argument; in the sound_sensor mode the program polls the LM393 sound sensor on its digital output pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM) every 10 ms, treats a logic 0 on this active‑low pin as a sound event, and publishes an alert on a ZeroMQ socket bound to tcp://*:5555 using the topic SOUND_ALERTS, while in the alarm_node mode the program subscribes to tcp://localhost:5555 for the same topic and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second; the implementation must use the GPIO bus directly without any driver library, provide robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses an IR receiver such as the TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) to decode NEC infrared remote signals and report the decoded commands both to syslog and to an MQTT broker at localhost on port 1883 using the topic ir/decoded, publishing the command as a JSON object; the program must register an alert callback on the falling edge of the GPIO to capture pulse timings, interpret the NEC frame consisting of a 9 ms mark followed by a 4.5 ms space header, 560 µs marks for each bit, a 1690 µs space for logic‑1 and a 560 µs space for logic‑0, decode the full 32‑bit frame, validate the command against its inverted copy while allowing extended NEC frames that omit inverted‑address validation, check driver initialization and GPIO setup failures, guard against pulse‑buffer overflow, verify the NEC checksum, initialize the MQTT client once at startup and invoke the network loop in the main loop, and ensure clean release of all resources—including the driver, MQTT client, and syslog—when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.
